abstract: We study the problem of fair allocation when agents have dichotomous submodular preferences over groups of, rather than individual, items. These preferences naturally extend existing models, and have a natural interpretation in settings such as course allocation. We show that this seemingly minor extension results in computational intractability barriers: computing a utilitarian or Nash-optimal allocation with item complements is NP-hard. However, when agents' complementary bundles have size at most $k$, there exist poly-time algorithms that compute $\frac1k$-$\texttt{maxUSW}$ allocations and approximate Nash-welfare-maximizing allocations. While PO+EF-1 allocations may not exist in the complementary preference setting, it is possible to compute $\frac1{k+1}$-approximately $\texttt{maxUSW}$ EF-X allocations in polynomial time; furthermore, these allocations offer each agent $i$ a utility of at least $\frac{\texttt{MMS}_i - k}{k+1 + \frac1n}$, where $\texttt{MMS}_i$ is agent $i$'s maximin share guarantee. While the standard dichotomous binary submodular setting admits simple sequential techniques for computing fair and efficient allocations, our results for the complements setting require more complex tools from combinatorial optimization.

title: Fair Allocation with Dichotomous Preferences over Item Complements
